title: Debiasing Synthetic Data Generated by Deep Generative Models
summary: Shows that estimates computed on synthetic tabular data inherit a bias from the generator that ordinary corrections miss, and gives a debiasing strategy that restores root-n convergence of the standard error and returns confidence-interval coverage close to nominal, demonstrated in a simulation study and two clinical case studies. The strategy is generator-agnostic but is developed and evaluated entirely on CTGAN and TVAE, trained at the default hyperparameters of Synthcity in the simulations and of the SDV package in the case studies.
evidence: section 1 states that although the strategy is generator-agnostic the analyses focus on two DGMs for tabular data, CTGAN and TVAE (Xu et al., 2019); section 4.1 trains both on 250 replicates at sample sizes from 50 to 5000 and section 4.2 reports that the DGMs were trained with the default hyperparameters of the package Synthcity, with the SDV defaults (Patki et al., 2016) reported in appendix A.7.4 and used for the headline case-study results after the Synthcity settings gave biased estimates; appendix A.7.2 records that both packages implement CTGAN and TVAE as originally proposed by Xu et al. with a cluster-based normaliser for numerical features, and Tables A1 and A2 compare the two packages' defaults hyperparameter by hyperparameter

title: Synthetic Tabular Data Generation for Imbalanced Classification: The Surprising Effectiveness of an Overlap Class
summary: Splits the majority class into a clear part and an overlap part lying on the minority boundary, trains a class-conditional generator on the resulting three-way labels, and then drops the overlap class when assembling the classifier's training mix, reporting consistent gains for imbalanced tabular classification across four datasets and five classifiers. The procedure is applied on top of five generators, CTGAN among them, which is run conditionally on the ternary labels and reported both with and without the treatment.
evidence: section 2 introduces CTGAN (Xu et al. 2019) as the GAN-based tabular generator and section 5 names it first among the five generation methods the treatment is demonstrated over, alongside CTAB-GAN+, TabDDPM, ForestFlow and TabSyn; the method section states the pre-processing identifies an overlap set and then trains a conditional generator on the ternary labelled data, so CTGAN's own conditional mechanism carries the treatment without architectural change; the results tables report paired CTGAN and CTGAN ORD rows across Adult, Cardio, Fintech and Heloc. The named variant the paper coins, CTabSyn, is built on TabSyn rather than on CTGAN

title: Beyond the convexity assumption: Realistic tabular data generation under quantifier-free real linear constraints
summary: Introduces the Disjunctive Refinement Layer, which maps a generator's output into the region defined by quantifier-free linear formulas, so that background knowledge expressing non-convex or disconnected admissible spaces is satisfied by construction rather than by rejection sampling; constraint satisfaction becomes guaranteed and downstream efficacy improves. The layer is attached to five deep generative models, CTGAN and TVAE among them, giving CTGAN+DRL and TVAE+DRL, which are compared against the unmodified models and against the earlier linear-inequality layer from the same group.
evidence: the experimental section states that five DGMs are considered, WGAN, TableGAN, CTGAN (Xu et al., 2019), TVAE (Xu et al., 2019) and GOGGLE, and that DRL is built on top of each to create DGM+DRL models; the results tables report CTGAN, CTGAN+RS, CTGAN+LL and CTGAN+DRL and the matching TVAE rows across five datasets, and Figure 4 plots real, TVAE, TVAE+LL and TVAE+DRL samples in the constrained region; the introduction adopts machine learning efficacy (Xu et al., 2019) as the performance measure. Importance 4 rather than 5 follows the constrained-DGM precedent: CTGAN is one of five interchangeable substrates for a model-agnostic layer, not the thing being extended, and the paper is the successor to Stoian et al. (2024) already in the index

title: What's Wrong with Your Synthetic Tabular Data? Using Explainable AI to Evaluate Generative Models
summary: Turns synthetic-data evaluation into an explanation problem: a discriminator is trained to tell real records from synthetic ones, and feature importance, feature effect and counterfactual methods are then applied to that discriminator to say which columns, value ranges and interactions the generator got wrong, rather than returning a single quality score. CTGAN is one of six synthesizers whose detectability is compared, and the appendix works the full diagnosis through on ten CTGAN-generated nursery datasets.
evidence: Figure 1a compares detection accuracy for data from synthpop, ARF, CTAB-GAN+, TVAE, CTGAN and TabSyn under logistic regression, random forest and XGBoost detectors; section 5 states that appendix A repeats the exercise for synthetic nursery data generated with CTGAN [32], describing CTGAN as a widely used GAN-based generative model for tabular data and reporting that an XGBoost detector was tuned by Bayesian optimisation on each of ten CTGAN-generated datasets, with Figure 8 giving the permutation-importance and TreeSHAP interaction values for them

title: Pre-Tactical Flight-Delay and Turnaround Forecasting with Synthetic Aviation Data
summary: Asks whether synthetic flight records can stand in for proprietary operational data in pre-tactical delay and turnaround forecasting, training four generators on 1.74 million European flights and then comparing train-on-real against train-on-synthetic across five regression algorithms and three prediction tasks, and finds 94 to 97 percent of real-data predictive performance is retained. Two of the four generators are SDV code: CTGAN, whose mode-specific normalization the paper singles out for the multimodal delay distributions, and a Gaussian copula synthesizer, both carried in the companion library as adapted copies of sdv-dev sources over a declared RDT dependency.
evidence: phase 2 of the experimental framework trains four generative models on the real training data, Gaussian Copula, CTGAN [8], TabSyn and REaLTabFormer, reference [8] being Xu, Skoularidou, Cuesta-Infante and Veeramachaneni; the model description credits CTGAN's mode-specific normalization for handling delays that cluster around zero with a long tail, and Table II reports KS Complement, Chi-Squared, correlation and likelihood fidelity scores for all four. The companion repository named in footnote 1, github.com/SynthAIr/syntabair, carries src/syntabair/generators/ctgan and .../copula, whose header records the code as adapted from github.com/sdv-dev/CTGAN under the Business Source License, and declares rdt as a dependency in pyproject.toml
needs: the companion library SynthAIr/syntabair is itself an index candidate as a vendored_source repository and is not yet in the pool; the paper's Gaussian copula and fidelity metric names read as SDV and SDMetrics but the paper text credits neither, so the sdv-dev attribution here rests on the repository rather than on the paper

title: Large Language Models for Imbalanced Classification: Diversity makes the difference
summary: Oversamples the minority class by prompting a fine-tuned language model and then interpolating between generated and majority records, arguing that the diversity of the added samples matters more than their proximity to the real minority, and reports the best or second-best classifier accuracy on eight of ten datasets. CTGAN and TVAE are the two generative baselines among eight oversamplers, run from the sdv-dev implementation, with CTGAN the strongest competitor throughout the comparison.
evidence: section 4 lists eight oversampling baselines in three groups and places CTGAN [30] and TVAE [30] as the generative-based methods between the classical SMOTE family and the LLM-based methods, footnote 3 giving github.com/sdv-dev/CTGAN as the source code used; the results describe CTGAN as the runner-up and later the best baseline, report the proposed method's close-probability and coverage scores against CTGAN's, and Figure 5 sweeps the interpolation ratio against CTGAN as the reference line
